name: E. coli Two-Component Signaling
description: Escherichia coli utilizes Two-Component Signaling (TCS) systems as a primary mechanism to sense and respond to diverse environmental stimuli, crucial for its survival, adaptation, and pathogenicity. A typical TCS comprises a sensor Histidine Kinase (HK) and a cognate Response Regulator (RR). Upon perceiving an extracellular signal, the HK autophosphorylates, then transfers the phosphate group to the RR. The phosphorylated RR (RR-P) subsequently binds to specific DNA sequences, modulating gene expression to trigger appropriate cellular responses. This computational flowchart details the general TCS mechanism and integrates specific pathways. The Rcs system (Prüß BM, Cho SH) responds to envelope stress, influencing biofilm formation and motility. The Cpx system (Cho SH) also senses envelope stress, promoting the expression of chaperones and proteases for protein quality control. The RstAB system (Yao T) is activated by acidic conditions, particularly within macrophages, enhancing virulence and facilitating pathogen survival. These interconnected systems enable E. coli to adapt to varied niches, from free-living environments to host-specific microenvironments, as highlighted by niche-specific requirements (Brannon JR), underscoring their critical role in E. coli's biology and pathogenesis.
